rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The varieties of badiʿ are numerous, so Bāqillānī gives selected examples rather than an exhaustive catalogue.
rows.anchor: ووجوه البديع كثيرة جدا فاقتصرنا على ذكر بعضها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the claim that these ornamental devices prove Qurʾānic inimitability: once identified, they can be learned and deliberately practiced, like poetic composition.
rows.anchor: وليس كذلك عندنا لأن هذه الوجوه إذا وقع التنبيه عليها أمكن التوصل إليها بالتدريب والتعود والتصنع لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavily ornamented lāmiyya of Abū Tammām shows that poets can deliberately fill a poem with crafted rhetorical devices.
rows.anchor: حتى حشي جميع شعره منها واجتهد أن لا يفوته بيت إلا وهو يملؤه من الصنعة كما صنع أبو تمام في لاميته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The letters opening sūras include half the letters within several Arabic classifications, including strong versus nonstrong and emphatic versus open letters.
rows.anchor: وقد علمنا أن نصف هذه الحروف في جملة تلك الحروف المبدوء بها في أوائل السور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because later classifiers found this balanced selection in the sūra openings, its placement is beyond chance and signals divine knowledge of the unseen.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز أن يقع إلا من الله عز وجل لأن ذلك يجري مجرى علم الغيوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether Arabic was divinely instituted or formed by convention, the ordered structure of its letters is remarkable and reflects wisdom beyond ordinary capacity.
rows.anchor: فإن كان أصل اللغة توقيفا فالأمر في ذلك أبين وإن كان على سبيل التواضع فهو عجيب أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In alif-lām-mīm, alif is articulated farthest away, lām midway, and mīm at the lips; naming them signals the full range of familiar letters used in the Qurʾānic composition.
rows.anchor: لأن الألف المبدوء بها هي أقصاها مطلا واللام متوسطة والميم متطرفة لأنها تأخذ في الشفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses fire episode is told in varied forms across Ṭā Hā, al-Naml, and al-Qaṣaṣ; this range of narrative expression makes the challenge to produce a comparable discourse more comprehensive.
rows.anchor: لعلي آتيكم منها بقبس أو أجد على النار هدى

words: نُودِيَ أَنۢ بُورِكَ مَن فِى ٱلنَّارِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call of blessing and glorification flows into the following account of divine lordship and the signs of Moses’ staff and hand, with no break in the composition.
rows.anchor: فلما جاءها نودي أن بورك من في النار ومن حولها وسبحان الله رب العالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every word is beautiful and meaningful on its own, while the words become still more impressive through their precise arrangement and the smooth transitions between stories and sections.
rows.anchor: كل كلمة لو أفردت كانت في الجمال غاية وفي الدلالة آية فكيف إذا قارنتها أخواتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A skilled writer can test the claim by paraphrasing one Qurʾānic story and comparing the obvious loss in the substitute wording.
rows.anchor: فإن كنت من أهل الصنعة فاعمد إلى قصة من هذه القصص وحديث من هذه الأحاديث

rows.speaker: معاوية بن أبي سفيان
rows.claim: At death, Muʿāwiya learns that Quraysh rejoice at his impending death; in his ensuing sermon he condemns a corrupt age, distinguishes powerless wrongdoers, armed predators, religious hypocrites, and false ascetics, contrasts them with persecuted believers, and urges detachment from worldly life.
rows.anchor: قال الراوي لما حضرته الوفاة قال لمولى له من بالباب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurʾānic verse endings may resemble the rhyme positions of sajʿ, but that resemblance does not make the Qurʾān sajʿ.
rows.anchor: الحروف التي وقعت في الفواصل متناسبة موقع النظائر التي تقع في الأسجاع لا يخرجها عن حدها ولا يدخلها في باب السجع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sajʿ with uneven clauses, such as two words in one section and four in another, is condemned as unbalanced and ineloquent.
rows.anchor: وقد بينا أنهم يذمون كل سجع خرج عن اعتدال الأجزاء فكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Qurʾān were sajʿ, opponents could answer with balanced sajʿ and claim superior eloquence; its movement between forms shows its composition follows another principle.
rows.anchor: فلو رأوا أن ما تلى عليهم من القرآن سجع لقالوا نحن نعارضه بسجع معتدل

rows.speaker: النظام وعباد بن سليمان وهشام الفوطي
rows.claim: Bāqillānī argues that accepting sajʿ in the Qurʾān entails the view of al-Naẓẓām, ʿAbbād ibn Sulaymān, and Hishām al-Fuwaṭī that its composition is not inimitable and people were merely diverted from opposing it; he rejects that consequence.
rows.anchor: ولا بد لمن جوز السجع فيه وسلك ما سلكوه من أن يسلم ما ذهب إليه النظام وعباد بن سليمان وهشام الفوطي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speech from a fitting source and subject has a natural grandeur, whereas artificial imitation reveals estrangement and confusion.
rows.anchor: والشيء إذا صدر من أهله وبدا من أصله وانتسب إلى ذويه سلم في نفسه وبانت فخامته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Nuwās suits wine and drinking, while Dhū al-Rumma suits wilderness, camels, and pastoral life; Bāqillānī faults Abū Nuwās for treating ruins and wild animals.
rows.anchor: نعرف في شعر أبي نواس أثر الشطارة وتمكن البطالة وموقع كلامه في وصف ما هو بسبيله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Nuwās’ poem beginning with descriptions of ruined dwellings illustrates his poor fit for that subject, unlike his treatment of wine.
rows.anchor: عيب أبي نواس التصرف في وصف الطلول والرباع والوحش

rows.speaker: براكوية الزنجاني
rows.claim: Baraqawiyya al-Zanjānī recounts a poet reciting a ruin-themed poem to Hilāl ibn Yazīd on al-Aʿshā’s meter, then gives a quip about a young man from Zanjān mourning a ruin.
rows.anchor: سمعت براكوية الزنجاني يقول أنشد بعض الشعراء هلال بن يزيد قصيدة على وزن قصيدة الأعشى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The examples show that each kind of expression has a proper source and domain, and its fit reveals the nature of what produced it.
rows.anchor: وإنما ذكرت لك هذه الأمور لتعلم أن الشيء في معدنه أعز وإلى مظانه أحن وإلى أصله أنزع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book is deliberately concise because a full account of the Qurʾān’s qualities would be vast; even a brief exposition can indicate the method and guide readers to the proof.
rows.anchor: والذي سطرناه في الكتاب وإن كان موجزا وما أملينا فيه وإن كان خفيفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a subject is exalted, excessive elaboration can become inept and description can fall short.
rows.anchor: متى عظم محل الشيء فقد يكون الإسهاب فيه عيا والإكثار في وصفه تقصيرا

rows.speaker: الحكيم
rows.claim: A sage says an orator becomes tongue-tied when describing passion or a beloved, illustrating how difficult eloquent description can be.
rows.anchor: قال الحكيم وقد سئل عن البليغ متى يكون عييا فقال متى وصف هوى أو حبيبا

rows.speaker: أعرابي
rows.claim: A lost Bedouin guided by moonlight hesitates whether to pray that the moon be raised, illuminated, or beautified, since each quality is already present.
rows.anchor: وضل أعرابي في سفر له ليلا وطلع القمر فاهتدى به فقال ما أقول لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People differ in intellect, understanding, and knowledge; rhetorical criticism is especially difficult because it depends on subtle, deep, and varied forms of expertise.
rows.anchor: ولولا أن العقول تختلف والأفهام تتباين والمعارف تتفاضل

rows.speaker: المتنبي
rows.claim: Al-Mutanabbī’s lines say that readers may blame a sound statement because of poor understanding and receive poetry according to their aptitude and learning.
rows.anchor: أنشدني أبو القاسم الزعفراني قال أنشدني المتنبي لنفسه القطعة التي يقول فيها

rows.speaker: البحتري
rows.claim: Al-Buḥturī’s poem says poetry can move people who would not feel a sword blow, while the poet cannot make fools understand his crafted verse.
rows.anchor: أنشدنا الحسن بن عبد الله قال أنشدني بعض مشايخنا للبحتري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since judging all the varieties of human speech is difficult, assessing the speech of the Lord is more demanding still; those who count only ten forms of eloquence grasp little of it.
rows.anchor: فإذا كان نقد الكلام كله صعبا وتمييزه شديدا والوقوع على اختلاف فنونه متعذرا وهذا في كلام الآدميين

rows.speaker: جبير بن مطعم
rows.claim: Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim says that while hearing the Prophet recite al-Ṭūr in the dawn prayer, he feared the punishment after hearing that it would surely come, and then accepted Islam.
rows.anchor: ما روي في الحديث أن جبير بن مطعم ورده على النبي في معنى حليف له أراد أن يفاديه

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: A second report says that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb accepted Islam after hearing Sūrat Ṭā Hā.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث آخر أن عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه سمع سورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the opening of Fuṣṣilat was revealed about leading Quraysh; when the Prophet recited its warning of a thunderbolt like that of ʿĀd and Thamūd, ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿa sprang up in fear and could not answer.
rows.anchor: نزلت في شيبة وعتبة ابني ربيعة

rows.speaker: عثمان بن مظعون
rows.claim: ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn interprets ʿUtbah’s inability to answer after hearing the recitation as evidence that it comes from God.
rows.anchor: فقال له عثمان بن مظعون لتعلموا أنه من عند الله إذا لم يهتد لجوابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to grant protection until a polytheist hears God’s word makes hearing itself a proof against him, showing that recitation can establish the argument on its own.
rows.anchor: فجعل سماعه حجة عليه بنفسه فدل على أن فيهم من يكون سماعه إياه حجة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Different responses to recitation do not refute its evidentiary force: hearers had distinct obstacles, including doubt about God, divine unity, or prophethood.
rows.anchor: قيل له لا يجب ذلك لأن صوار فهم كانت كثيرة منها أنهم كانوا يشكون

rows.speaker: أبو سفيان بن حرب
rows.claim: At the conquest, Abū Sufyān professed that there is no god but God but admitted uncertainty about the Prophet’s messengership, illustrating one such obstacle.
rows.anchor: ألا ترى أن أبا سفيان بن حرب لما جاء إلى رسول الله ليسلم عام الفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayān has four forms—speech, condition, gesture, and sign—and people differ in their degree of clarity; the verse about God teaching bayān exemplifies this capacity.
rows.anchor: وأما حسن البيان فالبيان على أربعة أقسام كلام وحال وإشارة وعلامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opposite of clear expression is inability to communicate; the tale of Bāqil, who loses a gazelle while trying to indicate eleven with his fingers and tongue, illustrates it.
rows.anchor: ونقيضه العي ومنه قيل أعيا من باقل سئل عن ظبية في يده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some locate Qurʾānic inimitability in badiʿ devices or listed forms of eloquence; Bāqillānī distinguishes learnable techniques, which cannot prove inimitability, from rhetorical qualities inaccessible to learning and practice.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من زعم انه يأخذ ذلك من هذه الوجوه التي عددناها في هذا الفصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Simile is a recognized form of eloquence, but it is not independently miraculous: Ibn al-Muʿtazz also composed striking, almost magical similes.
rows.anchor: وأنت تجد في شعر ابن المعتز من التشبيه البديع الذي يشبه السحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He accepts that inimitability may lie in sustaining the highest eloquence across every subject and connecting the whole discourse with exceptional artistry.
rows.anchor: إذا أتى في كل معنى يتفق في كلامه بالطبقة العالية ثم كان ما يصل به كلامه بعضه ببعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No isolated device—an oath, simile, paronomasia, or antithesis—constitutes Qurʾānic inimitability without the composition that joins it to the surrounding discourse.
rows.anchor: إنما ننكر أن يقول قائل إن بعض هذه الوجوه بانفرادها قد حصل فيه الإعجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The device of negation and affirmation sets a denial against a positive reply, as in the cited verse about rejecting and not rejecting another’s words.
rows.anchor: السلب والإيجاب & كقول القائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Metonymy and indirection include the cited image of a red woman whose sky is fertile and land barren, as well as laḥn al-qawl.
rows.anchor: الكناية والتعريض & كقول القائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reversal and exchange are illustrated by al-Ḥasan’s paired maxims and a poem reversing the relation between a jewel and a beautiful face.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك & العكس والتبديل & كقول الحسن إن من خوفك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾānic reciprocal wording about bringing night into day and day into night is another example of reversal and exchange.
rows.anchor: وقد يدخل في هذا الباب قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iltifāt interrupts the initial syntactic course and then returns to it smoothly; without the interruption, the wording would remain straightforward rather than an instance of this device.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الالتفاتات أنه اعترض في الكلام قوله سقيت الغيث ولو لم يعترض لم يكن ذلك التفاتا

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī identifies Jarīr’s sudden invocation of rain on al-bashām as an example of iltifāt.
rows.anchor: قال لي الأصمعي أتعرف التفاتات جرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jarīr’s address to the tents after asking when they were at Dhū Ṭulūḥ provides another iltifāt example.
rows.anchor: متى كان الخيام بذي طلوح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī’s parenthetical denial, ‘they lie,’ interrupts the line and then returns to its course as another example of iltifāt.
rows.anchor: ألا زعمت بنو سعد بأني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kathīr’s line about generous givers being taught delay by the beloved is cited as another instance of the device.
rows.anchor: لو أن الباذلين وأنت منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Tammām’s line turns from the addressed place to an appeal to the poet’s tears, supplying another example of iltifāt.
rows.anchor: وأنجدتم من بعد اتهام داركم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In another Jarīr example, the poet turns toward the pigeon and prays for it to remain among flourishing branches.
rows.anchor: طرب الحمام بذي الأراك فشاقني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The line can be construed as recalling the day the speaker slaughtered his mount or as linked back to the day at Dārat Jaljal; Bāqillānī calls its first hemistich foolish.
rows.anchor: تقديره اذكر يوم عقرت مطيتي أو يرده على قوله يوم بدارة جلجل وليس في المصراع الأول من هذا البيت إلا سفاهته

rows.speaker: بعض الأدباء
rows.claim: An adab critic says the phrase ‘O wonder’ refers to the young speaker’s slaughtering his mount for the women; Bāqillānī rejects this as far-fetched and unsupported by the wording.
rows.anchor: قال بعض الأدباء قوله يا عجبا يعجبهم من سفهه في شبابه من نحره لهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though critics praise the second hemistich’s simile, making ‘meat’ definite and ‘fat’ indefinite leaves unclear whether both describe the same animal and leaves one comparison undeveloped.
rows.anchor: انه عرف اللحم ونكر الشحم فلا يعلم انه وصف شحمها وذكر تشبيه أحدهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praising the quality of food served to guests may be criticized, though Arabs traditionally boast of it while Persians regard such boasting as shameful.
rows.anchor: وفيه شيء آخر من جهة المعنى وهو انه وصف طعامه الذي أطعم من أضاف بالجودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Comparing fat to silk is a commonplace image rather than an original device; the added word ‘twisted’ mainly supplies the rhyme and is not regarded by artisans as badiʿ.
rows.anchor: وأما تشبيه الشحم بالدمقس فشيء يقع للعامة ويجري على ألسنتهم فليس بشيء قد سبق إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Boasting about food given to loved ones is blameworthy, unlike permissible pride in feeding guests, unless the speaker uses joking or playful manner.
rows.anchor: أن تبجحه بما أطعم للأحباب مذموم وإن سوغ التبجح بما أطعم للأضياف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bāqillānī notes that some opponents call the Qurʾān fabricated and others call it borrowed ancient tales, while declining to list every challenge verse for brevity.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من يزعم أنه مفترى فلذلك لا يأتي بمثله ومنهم من يزعم أنه دارس وانه أساطير الأولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If any part of the Qurʾān could be written or fabricated by people, then the same could be done to all of it; the challenge shows that they failed to produce its like.
rows.anchor: ولو جاز أن يكون بعضه مكتوبا لجاز على كله ولو جاز أن يكون بعضه موضوعا لجاز ذلك في كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prolonged challenge made the Qurʾān a proof of prophethood and exposed its opponents to loss of life, property, and family; if able, they could have escaped these consequences through an easy counter in their own familiar language.
rows.anchor: لو كانوا يقدرون على تكذيبه لفعلوا وتوصلوا إلى تخليص أنفسهم وأهليهم وأموالهم من حكمه بأمر قريب هو عادتهم في لسانهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their great hostility and willingness to fight, debate, and leave their homeland make it implausible that they would forgo a simple verbal rebuttal if they could manage one; their failure demonstrates incapacity.
rows.anchor: فلما لم تحصل هناك معارضة منهم علم أنهم عاجزون عنها
